items.title: Who will actually ride the Giro d’Italia in 2027? Analysing the choices facing Pogačar, Vingegaard, Seixas, Evenepoel, Del Toro and more
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
With the routes for the 2027 editions of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia now out of the bag, the world's top general classification riders have all the material with which to make their Grand Tour plans for the season ahead.

Though the Vuelta a España shouldn't be forgotten about, the big question, as ever, is Giro or Tour – or even both.

But where does that leave the world's leading Grand Tour contenders in their decision-making processes for next year? And who will actually be swayed to target the Giro d'Italia over and above the Tour de France?

Here, we take a look at factors that will be swaying all the big names, and how likely they are to be booking a flight to Italy next May.

Highly unlikely

The Giro d’Italia organisers have dangled a carrot in front of Tadej Pogačar’s nose with two stages on Slovenian soil, but it doesn’t seem to have worked – at least not fully. The 2024 Giro champion sounds like he’d love to return for a second appearance but other duties might take precedence: “Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year,” he said recently.

The Vuelta, of course, is a source of unfinished business, given he crashed out while in the lead this year, and given it remains the missing Grand Tour in his trophy cabinet. Pogačar has demonstrated a penchant for broadening his palmarès and ticking races off in recent years, and for someone who has won so much, the Vuelta represents something of a gaping hole at this point. And given the Tour de France is an immovable point on his program, the Spanish Grand Tour is set to be the preferred combination.

When it comes to the Giro, another stumbling block would appear to be another missing piece of the Pogačar palmarès puzzle: Paris-Roubaix. The Slovenian has become one of the most prolific Classics riders of all time and the Hell of the North is now the only missing trophy in his Monument cabinet. Having finished runner-up two years in a row, an extraordinary and historic victory is clearly within his grasp, and this seems to have become a major fixation. The cobbled Classics in early April are less than a month out from the Giro and require completely different training loads and even physiologies – Pogačar himself opened up about the weight he gained for this year’s Spring campaign and hitting that flat-land Classics shape isn’t compatible with gearing the body for a mountainous three-week race.

Pogačar will surely return to the Giro in the future but it would be a huge surprise to see him there next year.

If Pogačar does indeed stick with his 2026 schedule, then that opens the door for Isaac del Toro to target the Giro d’Italia in a bid to win a first Grand Tour. The Mexican arguably should have won the 2025 Giro but let victory escape him in a hugely dramatic denouement, and he decided against trying to right those wrongs this year in favour of joining Pogačar at the Tour, where he joined him on the podium.

That ride this summer – along with the rest of an outstanding season – confirmed Del Toro as one of the very best riders in the world and a Grand Tour winner in waiting. Having gained that experience – and particularly having learned directly from Pogačar at the Tour – it would seem Del Toro is ready to step up into a true leadership role, and the Giro represents the perfect place for that to happen.

Going back to the Tour, meanwhile, would likely yield the very same result, so in terms of his development the Giro feels like a logical next step in 2027.

Unlikely

Only a few weeks ago, when the new Giro boss Luca Guercilena was talking about re-balancing routes and re-embracing time trials, it seemed like Remco Evenepoel would have a huge decision to make following his brilliant runner-up finish at this year’s Tour. Return to France, and knock against the impenetrable Pogačar-shaped door once again? Or head to Italy on a more favourable route with less competition?

But the route reveals have done away with those preconceptions. Given Evenepoel’s incredible time trialling superiority and his vulnerability to an off-day in the mountains – even if his 2026 Tour was impressively consistent – the Tour is surely the route that suits him the best next year.

He would dearly love to win the Giro – the first Grand Tour he took aim at in his career and which he arguably might have won in 2023 were it not for COVID-19 – but he won’t want to miss the Tour after what he did there this year, and now the route doesn’t really give him a convincing counter-argument.

The Tour also seems to sit better with Evenepoel’s season as a whole, allowing him to return to the Tour of Flanders after his impressive debut this year, and target a third Liège-Bastogne-Liège title later in the Spring, before building quietly towards the Tour like last year. There has been speculation over a Giro-Tour double but all the noise from the Evenepoel camp is that he’ll do even less racing – and even more tailored training blocks – in 2027, so this doesn’t seem realistic in the slightest.

Unlikely

Having won the Giro at a canter this year, and with it now ticked off on his palmarès amid the complete set of all three Grand Tours, the question is what Vingegaard has to gain by going to the Giro. Sportingly, not an enormous amount – another Giro title would still be an amazing achievement and one that would underline his greatness as a five-time Grand Tour winner. However, after a third straight Pogačar victory and with that once-dramatic rivalry now looking extremely one-sided, the Tour de France is surely more urgent a priority than ever.

The interesting point is that the Tour was still, on paper, the priority in 2026. Vingegaard spent the best part of the spring and summer talking about how he is stronger in the second Grand Tour of a season, making the Giro appear to be little more than a preparation race. We never got to see the theory truly play out, as Vingegaard – already far behind but still insisting he was growing into the race – crashed out of the Tour on stage 15.

If he and Visma-Lease a Bike truly believe his best Tour de France form can be reached with the Giro in the legs, then another double could well be on the cards, which would be great for the sport. But with the Giro ticked off the palmarès, the suspicion is that they will focus squarely on the Tour de France and opt for a more tailored approach – after all, as easily as Vingegaard won the Giro, it still comes with a lot of mental stress plus the exposure to 21 days where – as he and Pogačar know only too well from last year – best laid plans can be wiped out in a moment’s misfortune.

After placing fourth at this year’s Tour de France, in the middle of some truly sensational exploits in the spring and autumn, Paul Seixas is the hottest property in cycling and his Grand Tour choices for 2027 will be eagerly anticipated and indeed scrutinised.

The routes for both races suit the Frenchman but he’s like Pogačar – a Swiss Army knife all-rounder and perhaps even better against the clock – so it’s hard to envisage a route that wouldn’t suit his characteristics.

Does he go back to the Tour and try to get a little closer to Pogačar? Or does he take on the Giro with a much clearer path to victory?

Still only 20, there’s no way he’ll ride both, not least because he has his heart set on the World Championships near his grandparents’ house, which take place earlier next year, just a month after the Tour. In fact, those Worlds might just sway it, coming in a tricky spot not soon enough after the Tour to cash in on the residual form that follows the initial recovery period, and not long enough away to truly wind down and build back up again. In that sense, if Seixas is as serious as he sounds about the Worlds, doing the Giro and skipping the Tour would actually make the most sense in terms of peaking for both (even if it might compromise any Spring Classics ambitions).

One important thing to note with Seixas is that he has not yet finalised contract negotiations for 2028 and beyond. After turning pro on an initial three-year deal, and with his value skyrocketing, this is a huge next contract for Seixas and one that will shape the sport for the next five years. Decathlon are working hard to keep him but rumours of big-money offers have been doing the rounds all year. What all this means for the Giro is that Seixas finds himself in the unusual position of being the one who can call the shots. A French team with the star French rider usually means the Tour de France – it took years for Romain Bardet to be allowed to do the Giro in this same team – but Decathlon are so desperate to tempt him to stay that, when it comes to his race program in 2027, it’s essentially his own call.

  • have arguably the deepest Grand Tour arsenal in the world, and if Evenepoel does decide against the Giro then it will be interesting what the German team do with their marquee home talent, . With less time trialling, the Giro seems better suited to the 2025 Tour podium finisher, and there were some awkward moments of cohabitation with Evenepoel at last year’s Tour. had a disappointing Giro this year but could return as a home hope, while former winner might be tempted to do what he did this year – shoot for the podium at the Giro then work for Evenepoel at the Tour.
  • will almost certainly send to the Tour de France after he missed out on the chance this year, with Egan Bernal, Thymen Arensman and Carlos Rodríguez the others who'll need to fit around those plans. 
  • could well hand the Giro reigns to the rider who guided Vingegaard so impressively in the mountains this year: . The 24-year-old Italian had a stand-out season and looks set to assume greater responsibility next year. 
  • have decisions to make with Giro runner-up joining and at the team. Gall has been the best of them in the past couple of years but really struggles against the clock, unlike the other two, so it could be Giro for the Austrian again.
  • was more of a stage hunter with EF but might renew his GC focus at given their lack of climbing options, perhaps we'll see him double up.

items.title: Zero to hero? Wind tunnel testing the new Look 795 Blade RS
items.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
items.content:
In a world of some fairly extreme aero machines being released, the Look 795 Blade RS looks almost conventional in its appearance.

Svelte tube profiles that rely on squared off ends for aero performance and more standard clean lines rather than sharp angles and flared elements result in a bike that looks like a rather normal bike.

Interestingly this is Look's out-and-out aero machine, but it doesn't resemble the deep profiled aero bikes from the likes of Factor, Van Rysel, or other brands. It does however have a rather narrow front profile, something the Factor ONE and Tarmac SL9 have all pursued with the leading edge of the bike often being one of the more important elements when it comes to overall aerodynamic performance of a bike.

The bike doesn't come with dedicated aero bottle cages, like the ENVE Melee V2 or Trek Madone, but the bottle boss placement and tube shapes are designed to limit the negative impact that fitting a 500ml round bottle tends to have an aerodynamic performance.

Tyre clearance is claimed to be 34mm, while Look states that the bike can come in at 7kg fully race ready. What that means is not specified, but we'd hope that means with bottle cages, computer mount, and pedals fitted.

We're now somewhat dab handed when it comes to conducting these wind tunnel tests and for this latest round we followed the same protocol as previously.

We're already outlined in great detail how we went about testing in our 2025 aero bike shootout article if you want to go over it in all it's glory there.

However I'll outline the main principles here as well.

This is the first test, and involves the bike being tested as stock with the wheels that it comes with and all components as standardised as we can.

The position is adjusted to be as close as possible between bikes in terms of size, handlebar width, stack, and seat height, but the saddle, groupset, and all the components are as sold.

This allows us to test the bike as is without the added complexity of a riders legs acting as large moving pistons disrupting the airflow. Although not attributable to real world, it can show some interesting differences between bikes that may have data that suggests they are fast, but not necessarily in the real world where a rider is present.

Obviously no bike can be ridden without a rider, so testing with a rider present on the bike is essential for actual real world applicable testing that matters to you.

Some bikes are designed with riders on them, while others are not. Comparing the two tests can give us an indication of who has followed certain design methodologies.

The only issue is that, even while keeping rider position as consistent as possible, it is difficult to keep the margin of error as small as the frame-only. The margin for error is greater, yes, but still gives us a good idea of good performing bikes, bad performing ones, and standout offerings.

  1. Bike only, control wheels

Wheels make up a descent amount of aero performance for a bike as they are one of the first things the air hits and the last that it leaves.

We use a standardised set of wheels (Enve SES 4.5) and tyres (28mm Continental GP5000 S TR) because some of the test bikes come with 40mm wheels and 28mm tyres, while others came with 60mm options and 30mm tyres. There is also the fact that some frames are designed to perform best with certain wheels, while others are not.

Testing with a control set of wheels allows us to test the frame, fork, and components in isolation somewhat to the effect of a synergistic wheelset.

We can also infer some wheel performance testing from doing this, as some wheels test worse than the control ones, and others better.

All testing was done across yaw angles (the angle the wind hits the bike) of -15°, -10°, -5°, 0°, 5°, 10° and 15° to allow us to assess crosswind performance.

Testing itself is conducted at 40km/h as a decided speed that the majority of buyers may expect to go on their faster-paced grouprides, group events, or giving a road bike time trial a go. Rather than the 45kph+ that WorldTour pros race. We appreciate everyone will go faster than this at points, but that'll mostly be with the support of a tailwind or a hill.

Bike-only tests collect data for 10 seconds at each yaw angle, as there is less noise (messy data) and variance here, while With-Rider tests are done for 30 seconds each time to reduce the amount of noise we get from the tests and reduce the error margin.

To try and standardise things we ensure all testing is done in the same gear, so rear mech placement is similar, and with the same front tyres as they are the first thing the wind impacts. Position on the bike is kept as close as possible between bikes thanks to a laser outline so body position has limited impact on the results.

Two Elite Vico cages with Elite Fly bottles are fitted to each bike, save for when the bike comes with aero bottle cages as standard such as the ENVE Melee V2. This is because those are included parts of a bike, and people are unlikely to remove them (in favour of something nominally worse) so it is worth testing them as part of the entire system.

We also still have our trusty Trek Emonda ALR control bike for the baseline testing. We test this at the start and end of each test day to ensure that conditions have remained consistent throughout the testing day. It hasn't changed since we started doing these tests, so allows us to ensure 2025 and 2026 testing days are comparable.

You can see here that the Look performs far better than our Emonda, and close to the Factor ONE. Look does state that the bike shaves 15 watts off the performance of the previous generation at 50kph, while performance across -15˚ to 15˚ Yaw was also an important part of development.

The Blade is actually closer to the performance of the Factor at the more extreme Yaw angles. Often more bladed tube shapes can perform well here acting as a sail, but only to the point at which they stall. Round tubes, like the Emoda, struggle here.

Total drag for the Look 795 Blade RS was 35.42 watts faster than the Emonda baseline. More impressively, it was a massive 11.3 watts faster than the previous generation 795 that we tested previously.

It also places it just shy of 5 watts behind the Factor ONE in first place for our bike-only testing.

When we add a rider to the equation, essential for the real world, performance is relatively better, with the Look actually beating the Factor at the more extreme yaw angles.

These are more prevalent at lower speeds, blustery conditions, and when riding in a bunch, so the bike seems well primed to perform well in more real world conditions.

However, we can see that the 2026 testing conditions were slightly faster than the 2025 based on the Emonda baseline testing, so although the Look performs well, it may be a watt or so slower than our measures when compared to previous test bikes.

With a rider present, the Look jumps up the table comfortably into the top quarter. 22.9 watts faster than the Emoda and just under 5 watts behind the Cervélo S5 at the top.

It's worth caveating that with a rider, not only is the error margin greater, meaning the bike could be anywhere from 3rd to near last, but the differences between frames are also smaller. The fact is that a rider makes up most of the drag, while large moving legs disrupt that smooth airflow massively.

This is why a clean front end and trailing edge can really help in real world aero performance, as well as deeper section wheels. It helps reduce the drag at the front of the bike, while also sometimes helping in smoothing the airflow coming off the back of the rider.

Interestingly, when we add the control wheels to the equation, the Look suffers badly, dropping down the table and 7.09w behind the Factor ONE and 2.72w slower than with the standard wheels.

This is likely due to the bike being tested initially with the Scope Artech 6 wheelset, which is deeper than our ENVE 4.5 control wheelset and a very sold aero performer as we have tested ourselves.

An intriguing aside, the Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro also came with the same wheels (albeit it modified versions to better suit the frame), yet it suffered less when we switched to the ENVE wheels. It looks like the Look does perform exceptionally well with those Scope Artechs.

This may look damning for the Look, but it's worth bearing in mind that the bike performed relatively better with a rider present than just the frame-only, which is how we tested the control wheels.

Even taking the same penalty of switching the wheels and applying this directly to the rider-on tests, the Blade 795 RS remains in the mid-table cluster which includes the likes of the 2026 Cannondale SuperSix Lab71 and aero focussed Van Rysel RCR-F.

Look designed this bike to be fast in the real world, with bottles mounted and a rider present. Given that the 795 Blade RS performed relatively better with a rider on the bike, we can say that to that end Look has done a very good job. It has also eclipsed the aero performance of the previous generation bike as a frame-only and rider-on model which is mightily impressive given the visually limited differences.

Some of the aero performance is clearly from being tested with a class-leading set of deep section 60mm wheels versus some bikes that were tested with 40mm options. However, even with that accounted for, it's a solidly performing bike.

A race-ready weight of 7kg claimed is also impressive and up there with all-rounder aero bikes that don't fully sacrifice light weight. My favourite addition to this bike though is the handlebar system.

On the face of it, it looks like a one-piece bar and stem, but the reality is that it is a very smooth and clean two-piece system. Given that many one-piece systems can cost in excess of £500 and be a pain to switch, this two-piece system offers easily adjustability to change reach and bar width.

The reason this is so helpful is that, as our tests have shown, the rider makes up the largest proportion of drag in the full bike and rider equation. Having the option to adjust the geometry more to accommodate a more aerodynamic position that can be sustained for a ride is going to offer a far larger potential aero gain than the small differences between frames.

items.title: Roval Rapide Sprint CLX wheelset review: Forward thinking depth optimised for ‘old school’ tyre widths
items.author: Ollie Smith
items.content:
• : £2,998, $3,398, €3,498
  • : 1395g (with valves & tape)
  • : Satin Carbon/Gloss Black (tested) or Gloss Carbon/Gloss White
  • : Front Rim Dimensions - Depth: 63mm, External Width (at widest point): 35mm, Internal Width: 21mm, Bead Hook Width: (4.3)mm, Rear Rim Dimensions - Depth: 58mm, External Width (at widest point): 34.4mm, Internal Width: 21mm, Bead Hook Width: (4.2)mm
  • : Carbon fibre rims & spokes, titanium spoke hardware, alloy nipples

Roval claims that the Rapide CLX Sprint are ‘the fastest road wheels [they’ve] ever tested’. When they were launched in the summer of 2025, they turned heads and raised eyebrows with their revolutionary (to the road market, at least) mullet dimensions; a deeper front wheel and shallower rear wheel.

A front wheel depth of 63mm and a rear wheel depth of 58mm, paired with carbon spokes and ceramic DT 180 hubs makes the intended use of this wheelset exceedingly clear; these are for racing. Fast.

I’ve been testing these wheels for the last few months on the road in pretty much all conditions. I’ve ridden them on fast flat group rides, up long mountains, and battered them over a broad variety of road surfaces from smooth asphalt to fine gravel on unpaved bike paths.

By way of comparison, I’ve actually ridden (and owned) both previous generations of Roval’s Rapide wheelsets, and currently use a set of Reserve 57/64 Turbulent wheels on my race bike - as well as having tested dozens of other wheels over the last few years; so I have a pretty deep pool of experience to compare with.

These Rovals are positioned as one of the best road bike wheels in the market, and have all the credentials - on paper, at least - to live up to Roval’s speed claims.

Let’s address the elephant in the room first; the difference in depth between the front and rear wheel is nowhere near as noticeable as you might think. At a glance, you’d be hard pushed to see a 5mm difference in rim depth when standing still - let alone when whizzing past - and when we first spotted these wheels at the Spring Classics in 2025, it was only the eagle eye of senior tech writer Will Jones - who really is frightfully attuned to 5mm differences in wheel depth - who spotted these on the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe bikes.

When explaining this design choice, Roval claimed that “90% of aero benefit comes from the front wheel”, so they optimised this whilst reducing the depth of the rear wheel to save weight and keep the overall package as light as possible. I can’t validate these aero claims myself, but the theory is sound. I’ll get into my experience with the performance of these wheels later on.

Depth aside, the rest of the rim dimensions are equally as interesting. Both front and rear internal widths are 21mm. This was somewhat of a surprise to me and - dare I say it - quite narrow for a modern wheelset. Roval’s reasoning for this width is that the rim profile is aerodynamically optimised around a 28mm tyre. For comparison, the Reserve 57|64 are 25.4mm internally at the front and 24.4mm at the rear - so are much better suited to more modern tyre widths of 30mm, 32mm, or even wider; not uncommon even on racing bikes in 2026.

My main surprise with the internal rim width is that it’s exactly the same as the previous two generations of Rapide wheels - which were first launched alongside the Specialized Tarmac SL7 in 2020. At the time, 21mm was plenty wide enough for the narrower widths riders chose back then - I was still racing on 23mm rubber - but a lot’s changed since then, and the choice to retain a 21mm internal width feels a little out of touch with the choices riders are making in 2026.

The wheels came to me in ‘review spec’, meaning they were missing a lot of the accessories they are supposed to include (such as wheel bags or tubeless valves), but they did come with a set of 28mm Specialized cotton folding racing only tyres. When mounted, these looked a lot narrower than 28mm, and left a noticeable lip of the rim showing. The external widths are 35mm at the front and 34.4mm at the rear, which accentuated how narrow the 28mm tyres looked, and they measured up closer to 27mm. Roval claims that the wheels are rated for tyres ranging from 24mm up to 38mm - I would suggest that the profile of a 38mm tyre on these rims would be sub-optimal, at least aerodynamically.

After a few weeks on the 28mm cotton tyres with inner tubes (which were amazing by the way - these were my race tyres of choice a few years ago, and it was lovely to revisit them and remind myself how fast and chattery they feel compared to modern, fatter rubber) I switched to some tubeless options; namely Continental’s GP5000 S TR in a 30mm and then a 32mm spec. I’ll get onto how this impacted the wheels in the performance section of the review.

At this point, it’s worth noting that the Rapide range of wheels are available in three specifications; the CLIII, the CLXIII, and these Sprint CLX. The CLIII and CLXIII both use a shallower rim combination of 51mm at the front and 48mm at the rear. All three variants share the same carbon rim construction, with the differences being the choice of spokes and hubs specced. The CLIII are priced at £1,548 and use DT Swiss Competition Race Straight Pull spokes and DT Swiss 350 stainless steel hubs, and the CLXIII uses the same spokes and hub combo as these sprints and are priced the same at £2,998.

Carbon spokes are still fairly rare on stock wheels from mainstream brands, but Roval has plumped for composite spokes manufactured by Arris Composites.

Arris is a brand I wasn’t familiar with before diving into the spec sheet of these wheels, but a quick glance at its website shows that it primarily produces ‘drone & defense’ products, alongside carbon plates for running shoes. In the interest of brevity, I won’t be diving too much further down the rabbit hole beyond their company motto: “Making products radically lighter and stronger”. Safe to say, it delivers on these goals.

The front wheel has 18 two-cross radially laced spokes, and the rear 24 one-cross / three-cross. All the spokes have alloy nipples and titanium endpieces.

I haven’t used carbon spokes before, and to be honest I don’t think I noticed that much of a difference. Of course, they’ll contribute to the feather light weight of these wheels, but in terms of stiffness or compliance, I can’t say they moved the needle for me compared to other wheels with steel spokes. I did have thoughts of their fragility in the back of my mind for the first few rides, but these quickly vanished after battering over a few cobbled sectors around Bristol and having no issues. In terms of practicality, they are pretty proprietary spokes, but Roval supplies four extra spokes and nipples should anything happen.

Roval has specced the ‘Sprint’ variation of these Rapide wheels with some pretty bling hubs. The hub body is a custom machined Roval alloy hub loaded with DT Swiss 180 ceramic bearings. These are really beautiful hubs that look as premium as they feel - even down to the minimalist centrelock rotor hubs with fewer splines to further reduce weight.

Riding with these wheels felt great. The combination of deep, aerodynamic rims picking up the wind and pushing me along like a sail combined with the low rotational weight and super smooth hubs gave me the sensation of having really good legs on every ride. Those subtle sensations - when you punch over the top of a climb and get back up to speed a little quicker than normal, or when you look at your speed on the flat and find your going a few kilometers an hour quicker than you thought you were - are hard to find when you’re an experienced rider and usually ride pretty fast equipment, but these wheels really did feel special.

Of course, there’s every chance that this was the placebo effect of having some shiny new equipment, but it didn’t really diminish much throughout the test period, so I’m inclined to say the wheels are actually just really fast.

They were stiff without being jittery, deep without being easily led by crosswinds, and light enough to flick up climbs out the saddle without the sensation of being dragged backwards that some aero wheels can have.

I rode these wheels in some pretty heavy rain throughout the testing, and - although I haven’t put thousands of kilometers into them - the hubs are still running smoothly and showing virtually zero signs of wear.

Gushing aside, I did have one qualm with the wheels that I couldn’t shake. Using the 28mm inner-tube-only cotton tyres pumped up to about 80psi felt a bit jittery; they were firm and translated a lot of road noise through to my hands. I didn’t necessarily mind this - it’s about what I expected and reminded me of how bikes used to feel. I also knew that the narrower tyres are the specification the wheels are designed around, so running them was offering the maximum aerodynamic benefit; which I’m sure played some part in making these wheels feel so…zippy.

However, when I switched up to 30mm tyres, the wheels did feel slightly more muted. The profile of the tyres on the rims was also much wider than the 28mm Specialized tyres (which suggests to me that the Specialized tyres actually come up a little undersized) and had an ever so slight lightbulb looking profile to them, which I knew would impact the aerodynamics.

They were, of course, more comfortable than the 28mm tyre, but knowing they were costing watts and losing that real edge that these wheels had presented up until now didn’t feel great. The 32mm tyres were even wider, and ballooned out significantly from the rim.

Comparing this to the Reserve wheels I run day-to-day, which have a 25.4mm internal width at the front and 24.4mm at the rear and accept 30 and 32mm rubber with a much smoother profile, and the impracticality of the Roval’s rim width becomes clearer.

Race bikes have changed a lot in recent years. We’ve seen riders up-sizing their tyres for a number of years now, and not just in the Spring Classics where wider tyres have always been the norm. A wheel optimised for a 28mm tyres does make me think the Rapide Sprint CLXs will become outdated quite quickly as more and more riders follow the pros lead and switch to fatter rubber.

Now, I’m not suggesting there’s anything wrong with 28mm tyres, nor am I suggesting that there’s anything wrong with 21mm internal rim widths; much like rim brakes - they still work absolutely fine. But, you can’t deny, they are measurements that are becoming increasingly outdated as the industry progresses, and if you wanted to future proof yourself with a set of wheels that will stand the test of time, these probably aren’t quite wide enough to do so.

Personal preference aside, I’m pleased to say that the hooked rims were a doddle to set up tubeless with just a track pump using both the 30mm and 32mm Continental tyres.

If you plan on using these with inner tubes, make sure you stock up on long-valve spare tubes or valve extenders, as the 63mm front rim is too deep for most standard tubes, and you may get caught out…which DEFINITELY didn’t happen to me…

There’s no two ways about it; these wheels are expensive. Just under £3,000 is getting on for the most it’s possible to spend on stock wheels, and there are much less expensive wheels out there that will offer much of the performance you find in the Rapide CLX Sprints.

The Hunt 5AM Limitless wheels, reviewed by Will Jones recently, are a strong alternative. But even within Roval’s own Rapide range, the CLIIIs are £1,548 - almost half the price - and, although they lose the carbon spokes and drop down to a slightly shallower rim depth, will still be a significant upgrade on a lot of stock wheelsets.

However, these particular hoops are tricked out with some of thez finest components money can buy, and they feel wicked fast. Can you really put a price on that feeling?

Comparing them to the Reserve 57|64 SL Turbulent Aero wheels - which retail for a mere £1 more - and the spec sheet is broadly the same, bar the Reserve’s favouring a Tune hub. However, the Reserve wheels do include both the Shimano HG and the SRAM XDR driver in the box - so creep ever so slightly ahead on the value front. They also do have a more modern rim profile, so will hold their stock a bit better as the years roll on and tyres continue to get wider.

Overall, I really did enjoy riding these wheels, but I probably wouldn’t buy them. As fast and sprightly as they felt, I just wouldn’t want to part with that much cash for a rim of this width given my preference for more modern tyre widths.

You might disagree. If you’re a fan of (what I would call) narrower tyres and want a fast, stiff, light race wheel package, and are happy knowing that if you wanted to fit wider tyres to these wheels you’d be missing out on a lot of their claimed aero benefit, then these are great. If you want to run tyres wider than 28mm, I’d say there are better options out there.

Really well built package let down slightly by their less-than-modern internal rim width.

I wouldn’t change a thing with this build. Carbon spokes surprised me and the hubs are perfect.

These are lightning fast and make you feel like a better cyclist.

Incredibly light for a wheel of this depth, thanks to a premium no-holds-barred build.

Almost justifiably expensive given the spec sheet, but will be outdated pretty fast

items.title: Knicks 135, Bulls 105: Scenes from the World Champs looking like it
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
After 21 years at our Binghamton mansion, we’re moving. That means Mrs. Russell has countless extra chores for your intrepid blogger, including the retrieval of a loveseat in a sketchy neighborhood just before tip-off of tonight’s game between the Knicks (4-4) and the Bulls (1-7). Planning to watch the game after delivering the furniture to the new mansion (we are fabulously wealthy), I tried to ignore the alerts blowing up my phone. An impossible task. My eye caught “Jalen Brunson is on track to score 76 points” and “84 ties a franchise first-half record,” and all the surprise of tonight’s blowout was spoiled.

What did I see when I finally returned home? Brunson blazin’, OG Anunoby gorging at the free-throw line, KAT recording his eighth straight double-double, a very promising Dalton Knecht debut (10 PTS, 7 RBS, 16 MIN), solid minutes from Diawara, and a 44-point lead with 43% shooting from deep. We’ll need to burn sage around that loveseat to rid the stench of resentment. Final score: 135-105.

Landry Shamet started in place of Josh Hart (sore ankle) and scored the team’s first four points. From there, the Knicks went straight into high gear, turning a 6-6 tie into a 17-8 lead by attacking the paint and shooting with stunning efficiency. Who was the commander of the first-quarter onslaught? Captain Jalen Brunson, scoring his first 14 points on seven shots and finishing the frame with 22. That wasn’t his highest first-quarter total—he dropped 23 on Milwaukee in January 2025. Nonetheless, stunning. Cap had all but six of the Knicks’ first 19 points. Not to be kept in the corner, OG Anunoby contributed seven, including four from the stripe.

Mohamed Diawara checked in around the middle of the quarter, and this time he looked good! The sophomore delivered some of his best minutes yet this season, with a three and a block on Wilson’s layup. Fellow bench buddy Jordan Clarkson added five points, including a sweet transition three (dimed by Brunson). In a flash, the lead reached 22. Karl-Anthony Towns contributed just two points, starting slowly for his second straight game, but he helped in other ways, notching four boards, a steal, and an assist.

What’s your camp: “I Stand with Mikal” or “Mikal’s Got Me Sweating”? The struggling wing did little in the first quarter to calm our nerves about his recent play. He scored no points but dished two dimes and grabbed two boards.

For Chicago, Normal Norman Powell managed four points, while Tre Jones added four off the bench. Chicago got little from its young players, though. Rookie Caleb Wilson must’ve been star-struck in his MSG debut, missing all four of his shots, and Matas Bazookas went scoreless. At the break, the Knicks were sitting on a comfortable 43-21.

Q2: More of the same. Our heroes outscored Chicago 10-5 over the first three minutes to extend their lead to 53-26. The unrelenting Anunoby was still in beast mode, scoring six points and forcing two Josh Giddey turnovers. New York’s 3&D specialist scored 11 points in the quarter to reach 18 by halftime, while his three steals helped keep Chicago twitching and glitching.

With Brunson resting, Tyler Kolek ran the offense effectively, collecting four assists with sweet setups for Bridges, Clarkson, and Shamet. What a wonderful security blanket a skilled playmaker off the bench is. With Kolek dishing, Bridges racked up seven points. Diawara got into the action, too, scoring his first points of the season and finishing with seven first-half points.

Chicago managed a paltry little run early in the period, but New York responded with a 9-4 run that pushed its lead to 62-36—and eventually 78-41 with 1:47 left. Brunson added four points after returning, reaching 26 by halftime, while Towns remained quiet, adding just three more points in the second. You can count on KAT to crash the glass, though, and he did so for two more rebounds, giving him six at halftime. And newest ’Bocker Dalton Knecht made a fine first impression with a putback dunk and a step-back three-pointer for five points.

Chicago’s Josh Giddey had a particularly rough quarter, committing three turnovers in the opening three minutes, although he recovered to finish the half with seven points and four assists. Bahzelis finally got going late, scoring all six of his first-half points in the final 1:06, including a three-pointer with six seconds remaining. Wilson managed five points in the quarter, while Powell added just two, and Chicago found itself bereft of consistent scoring threats or prayers for winning this contest. Halftime score: 84-52. That tied New York’s franchise record for first-half points.

The Knicks had scorched the nets with 63% shooting from the floor and 50% from deep. The Bulls had shot 40% and a grotesque 19% from deep (5-of-26). The good guys also won the rebounding battle, 23-17, despite surrendering eight offensive rebounds, and committed just five turnovers to Chicago’s eight. Weirdly, the Bulls actually outscored the Knicks in the paint, 30-26, and attempted 13 more shots, yet trailed by 32 at halftime. Math was not my strong subject, but that doesn’t compute. Anyhoo, on to the second half!

Yet again, KAT pepped it up at halftime and came out firing. He drilled consecutive three-pointers in the opening minute as the home team goosed its lead to 36. Towns scored 12 points in the first five minutes of the quarter, including a putback layup, and reached another double-double with 17 points and 12 rebounds before heading to the bench.

Brunson added seven points, including a pull-up three, to reach 33 and call it a night.

The Bulls continued to fumble and bumble. Wilson missed his first three shots of the quarter and committed another turnover. Boozelis scored six points in the period, but the Bulls couldn’t make much headway against New York’s enormous lead. Meanwhile, Deuce McBride provided a spark off the Knicks’ bench, picking off passes from Norman Powell and Wilson before hitting a transition three-pointer that extended New York’s lead to 42. McBride later converted a four-point play, giving him seven points in the quarter, while Mohamed Diawara contributed another blocked shot and continued to provide promising minutes on both ends. Brother, imagine if the Knicks could play Chicago every night. . . .

Tre Jones was Chicago’s most productive player late in the quarter, scoring eight points over the final 2:19, including a three-pointer and three free throws. His unit closed the period on a 12-2 run (the Knicks got a little sloppy), but New York still ended the quarter up 113-79.

Hey! Check out this Knecht kid, blocking Buddy Hield’s layup attempt in the closing seconds. It’s gonna be fun to watch him go on heaters in Westchester.

With the Knicks leading by 34 entering the fourth, the reserves got the run of the joint. Andre Drummond opened the quarter with an alley-oop, while Clarkson and Knecht knocked down threes. James Wiseman made the most of his 10 minutes, finishing with eight points, eight rebounds, and three blocks, including rejections of Giddey, Bewzelis, and Patrick Williams. More of that, please! Pacôme Dadiet added four points. The Bulls briefly cut the deficit to 32, but Wiseman answered with a putback dunk and Knecht followed with a jumper. New York’s offense slowed with the end-of-bench guys on the floor, and Chicago won the quarter 26-22, but who’s complaining?

Mo’s knitting a cozy recap to keep you warm. New York travels to Cleveland for a clash with the Cavs. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.title: 'We have already taken some incredible steps, but we are far from finished' – Unibet Rose Rockets add new head of racing as invite to Tour de France targeted
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Unibet Rose Rockets have welcomed on board a new head of racing as Aike Visbeek joins for the 2027 season. The team will aim for a Tour de France wildcard invite next year, after making their Grand Tour debut at this year's Giro d'Italia.

The 50-year-old Dutchman previously worked at Sunweb, SEG Racing Academy, Intermarché-Wanty, and, for half of the 2026 season, Lotto-Intermarché.

He surprisingly departed Lotto at the end of June, wanting to spend time with his family after the death of his father-in-law. Now, he's heading for a new start next season with the Dutch ProTeam.

"What attracted me to the Rockets is that this is a team that is still building and has a clear ambition to keep moving forward," Visbeek said upon signing with his new team.

"I have been fortunate to work on similar projects before, where you really have the opportunity to develop something together."

Visbeek has more than a decade of experience in various roles across several teams, with his longest stint coming at Sunweb between 2013 and 2019. At Lotto, he worked as chief performance officer.

Unibet Rose Rockets chief sports officer Eelco Meenhorst said that Visbeek has "an impressive track record of developing teams and improving performance at the highest level.

"His knowledge, strategic insight, and experience will be extremely valuable as we continue to strengthen our performance," he added.

Unibet will field a largely similar squad for 2027, with only Axel Mariault (CIC Pro Cycling Academy) confirmed on the incoming list to date. Major names including Dylan Groenewegen, Wout Poels, and Lukáš Kubiš stay on board, while several other riders – including Clément Venturini, Odd Christian Eiking, and Victor Lafay – are departing.

Visbeek's addition isn't the team's only behind-the-scenes change this offseason. Bas Tietema, Unibet co-founder and main 'face', is stepping away from the sporting side to focus "even more on positioning the team as well as possible", including media and business duties, reported .

"The fact that [Visbeek] has chosen to join us says a lot about how far we have come as an organisation, but even more about where we believe we can go," said Tietema.

"We have already taken some incredible steps, but we are far from finished."

items.title: Amflow PX Carbon Pro e-MTB review: More power, more choice and a premium price tag
items.author: Jamie Darlow
items.content:
• £8,999 / $10,199 / €9,999
  • Fox Float 36 Factory, GRIP X2 damper, 160mm travel, 44mm offset
  • Fox Float X Factory, 210x55mm
  • Avinox M2S Drive Unit
  • Avinox Integrated Battery, 700Wh
  • Avinox SL alloy cranks, SRAM X0 Eagle AXS Transmission
  • Magura Gustav Pro, 4-piston callipers, Magura Sensor 203mm rotors
  • Amflow XMC-30 Carbon Mullet (29in front / 27.5in rear)

Amflow carries no legacy pedigree in the mountain bike world. Until mid-2024, the brand was virtually unheard of outside China. Formed under the umbrella of drone titan DJI to showcase its proprietary Avinox electric drive system, industry lore has it that Amflow was born only after established mountain bike brands turned down DJI’s motor partnership.

True or not, Amflow has bypassed the usual apprenticeship: it is already setting the benchmark the rest of the industry is scrambling to match. But does its PX Carbon Pro offer genuine trail dynamics, or is it merely an exercise in raw wattage?

What is now clear to me and many others is that Amflow is now one of the most desirable e-bike brands, thanks to its combination of power and performance. It now represents the industry standard that every other bike brand is playing catch-up to. But does this bike represent more than just the best watts-to-cash ratio of anything going? And can it match the established brands for ride feel and sheer joy?

The original Amflow (launched in 2024) was arguably a more radical step forward for e-bike design, introducing 1,000W of peak power and 120Nm of torque. The latest Amflow bike uses a new Avinox M2S Drive Unit that generates 150Nm of max torque (130Nm nominal) and 1,500W of peak power, which is unmatched by anything from Specialized, Bosch, Shimano, Bafang, Mahle, Fazua, Yamaha or Brose. In short – everyone else.

The Amflow range comprises three new models, all powered by the same DJI Avinox Drive System.

The PL weighs a claimed 19.2kg with a 2.27 kg carbon frame, 105 Nm continuous torque (120 Nm Boost), and 600Wh or 800Wh removable battery options. The PR is burlier, with heavier-duty FOX AWL HD/Float X suspension, SRAM Eagle Transmission, and Magura or Tektro brakes.

The range-topping PX I'm reviewing here has 150 Nm of torque, adjustable geometry (including chainstay lengths and head angles), a non-removable 700Wh battery, and SRAM X0 Eagle components.

You’ve probably heard plenty about the motor already, but it’s pivotal to understanding this bike and I can’t move on without filling in a few more details.

The Avinox M2S Drive Unit is almost exactly the same size as the M1 from the previous generation bike, which only makes the increased power claims more impressive still. Amflow says it’s also quieter than the old motor, while the 700Wh fixed internal battery has greater energy density and will outperform the older 800Wh version of old.

Fitting a 700Wh non-removable battery might seem like Amflow has shot itself in the foot by not giving riders the option to fit their desired battery size or swap out batteries for big ride days, but it worked for me. Without it, the extra complexity of a removable battery would have made the svelte downtube bigger - which not only looks ugly, but actually gets in the way on some bikes, reducing space for water bottles, gear, suspension components and even your knees.

I’d also argue you’ll never need a second battery on this bike. There’s no incentive to swap out the new 700Wh version for an older-designed 600Wh battery that saves just a few hundred grams. But more importantly, the fast charger took my flat battery from empty to full in around 90 minutes, so you could conceivably top it up at your lunch spot or from a mobile power bank.

While the Amflow name is relatively new, the four-bar linkage (Horst pivot) suspension design, with its telltale linkage on the chainstay, and general frame layout most certainly are not. It’s strikingly similar to bikes like the latest Specialized Stumpjumper Gen 3, YT Capra, Megamo Reason and many more bikes. It’s a sensible choice - long proven, easy for engineers to tune the suspension performance, and it leaves plenty of space around the bottom bracket and uninterrupted downtube for a big battery.

It uses a carbon fibre frame that Amflow says has 40 different geometry configurations in total, something we’ve seen before on bikes like the Stumpjumper. It has a choice of two bottom bracket heights, five head angles, and four chainstay lengths. You can run the bike with 29in front and rear, or as amixed wheel mullet using a 27.5in at the back. This adds complexity for Amflow, but it takes away any last-minute buying jitters about which wheel size to opt for.

This is the flagship bike for Amflow, and uses Fox Factory suspension components. It has a 160mm 36 fork with a GRIP X2 damper providing four-way high/low-speed compression and rebound adjustments, and a 210×55mm Float X shock with low-speed compression and rebound tuning.

That’s a lot more complexity than most of us need, but it means you can tinker and learn as you go. Using the smaller 36mm stanchioned fork with 160mm travel, and generating just 150mm travel through the rear wheel proves Amflow has done its research and will appeal to the majority of mountain bikers.

It has a wireless SRAM X0 Eagle Transmission setup, consisting of an X0 derailleur, XS-1295 10–52T cassette, X0 Flattop chain, an AXS Pod Rocker controller, and a 38T SRAM Direct Mount chainring on Avinox SL cranks (155mm on M/L, 160mm on XL/XXL). The rear derailleur is powered directly from the main e-bike battery via an internal Avinox power cable.

Four-piston Magura Gustav Pro hydraulic disc brakes paired with thick 2.5mm, 203mm Magura Sensor rotors front and rear. The bike rolls on an Amflow XMC-30 carbon mullet wheelset (29″ front with a 28H hub; 27.5″ rear with a 32H XD freehub) laced with SAPIM E-Light spokes. These are fitted with radial-carcass Schwalbe tyres: a 29×2.5″ Magic Mary Radial in Ultra Soft compound up front and a 27.5×2.5″ Albert Radial in Addix Soft compound at the rear.

I first rode an e-bike at Copper Mountain, Colorado, in 2013 and spent most of the ride giggling uncontrollably as I whined and wheelied past bemused riders. I then spent the next 10 years enjoying e-bikes in a more sombre, jaded journalist way. But I’m right back in 2013 with the Amflow, it’s a huge leap forward even from bikes with more than 100Nm of torque.

There are five power modes to choose from, and a boost button that will temporarily raise the torque to 150Nm for 30 seconds. There’s no limit to the number of times you can press this during a ride, except the ultimate limiting factor of the battery capacity and range. More on that in a minute.

I spent time in all five modes, and they’re genuinely useful. Set the power low enough and you can ride this e-bike with friends on naturally aspirated bikes… and really tedious a time you will have. I finished a ride like this recently, and proceeded to complete a second powered ride afterwards. If it sounds like I’m antisocial, it’s more that I can’t leave 700Wh of battery power burning a hole in my bike.

Set the power high enough and you’ve got the jump on everything you’re legally allowed to ride on a mountain bike. It will pick its way up the steepest of climbs, and on occasion I’ve used it to winch me straight back up the fall line tracks I’ve just descended… just because I can. And because it’s often the quickest way back up to the top.

Traditional e-bikes rely on frame-and-spoke magnets recording a single data point per revolution of the wheel. The Avinox system pairs with Magura’s Sensor rotor using an optical pick-up that measures 42 pulses per revolution. The resulting traction control is uncanny: instead of breaking traction and tearing up soft trails or scrabbling in the dust, the motor micro-modulates power delivery the instant wheel-slip is detected. Combined with a balanced front-end stack that prevents the front wheel from wandering, you can winch up technical, fall-line singletrack that would defeat almost any other machine.

The riding position suits this setup. There’s a 40mm high riser bar that shifts rider weight further backwards, but it’s not pronounced enough to stop me weighting the front wheel even when the winch uphill seemed impossibly vertiginous. I’m talking about those trails that have you hugging pressing yourself against the stem, as the front wheel hovers dangerously just a few inches from the ground.

As much as I enjoy climbing on the Amflow (and I really do, because it’s so easy and natural), I’m more interested in the descents. The motor cuts out at 25kph, like on any (UK and Euro) legal e-bike, but I’d hazard that most of us are under this threshold for most of the time when descending. It’s often either too steep or too tight. And it’s here I really noticed the beautiful way the DJI motor delivers its power - there’s a huge groundswell of support, but it’s never snatchy or unsettling, and it fires you out of a corner when you mess it up, or up a little rise in the trail to keep your speed up. It’s a lovely way to ride, keeping the bike fast and fluid, and a sensation I’ve honestly not had on any other e-bike.

Fox’s 36 Factory fork with the GRIP X2 damper strikes a sound balance between tracking and compliance, something I love on home trails in Surrey or rocky tech at BikePark Wales. I think the Amflow could easily justify the 38mm chassis of a Fox 38, the 36 saves a few hundred grams, and only fully formed enduro riders will miss the extra stiffness of a 38. Out back, I found that the Float X shock was supple in its initial stroke with a reassuring ramp-up through the mid-stroke. This let me run slightly deeper sag in the low BB setting without suffering harsh bottom-outs on squared-off square edges and drops.

It offers incredible grip and plenty of high-speed support to keep the bike nice and flat on janky stuff, but I did have to work hard to set it up perfectly, systematically winding on damping until I found the sweet spot. I think the Amflow could easily take a bigger 38 fork, which wouldn’t be out of place on a bike with enough stiffness like this one, but it adds weight, which is something Amflow has been keen to avoid on this bike, with its smaller 700wh battery and carbon bar and wheels.

The rear suspension is very good indeed. I found it beautifully supple when you’re charging over rough ground and feeling the trail under your wheels fly past, with the shock free and active and rear wheel eager to move out of the way of small rocks and roots. It’s also controlled and supportive when it’s time to slow it down and pick through rocks or over big roots, and I didn't have a harsh bottom out on drops or landings.

There’s a lot of support when you get to the mid-stroke, and that let me run more sag and drop the already-low BB down even further to improve the bike’s stability and cornering aplomb. The fantastically well-damped Schwalbe Radial tyres add to the grip and control this generates, taking some of the pressure off the bike’s suspension, and my hands. I didn’t like the Trail version of the Schwalbes on a previous bike, but the Gravity casing and Ultra Soft compound is probably the best tyre I’ve ridden in a long time.

It’s not just a low bike, though; it’s also slack (both the head angle and seat angle), and long. I kept the bike in its standard headset angle, because it’s still plenty slack enough even for proper enduro riding, and plonked the bike into its low BB setting for stability. For my kind of riding, the bike felt best with the longest chainstay setting, which seemed to calm the bike down on steeper trails. In the shortest setting, the rear wheel could break loose too readily.

This bike costs more than my car and my personal e-bike combined, and I would struggle to justify buying it. Price is subjective, though, and I think this is an astonishing machine for those who can drop nine grand on a mountain bike. The spec is fantastic - from Amflow’s own carbon wheels to the Fox Factory suspension - while the adjustable-geometry frame and ride feel show that Amflow have done their homework. And then there’s the motor, which other brands can’t touch right now.

That said, you can get a lot of the performance and most of the power from bikes lower in the Amflow range, or indeed other brands’ bikes using the M2S motor. When tested the entry-level original Amflow PL Carbon, Alan Muldoon said the basic in-line Fox shock was better than the Float X piggyback shock on the Pro model. I’ve yet to ride the entry-level, second-gen bike, but if they’ve got the tune right, there’s every chance it could pull off the same trick.

The Amflow has received so much praise online and on the socials that I wanted to hate it. But I absolutely fell in love with this bike. I’ve ridden scores of e-MTBs over the years and this one feels like nothing else. It’s so fast on singletrack and everything just short of full-on enduro tracks, where you come up against the inevitable - the end of its travel.

It reminds me of Whyte’s brilliant E-Lyte Evo. It’s comfortable and compliant in the same way, and absolutely razor sharp when cornering thanks to its brilliantly supportive suspension and geometry that means it can be whatever you want it to be.

It has a lot more power than the E-Lyte, though, much greater battery capacity, but the same light weight. And it’s here that the Amflow really makes the difference for me and noses ahead of other e-bikes: It’s stupidly good fun, easy to ride and move around, and forgives you when you mess up.

I said earlier the Amflow PX Carbon Pro is utterly soulless, and I love it for that. I have no idea who’s behind the DJI engineering, I don’t know where the bikes were designed and engineered, and which hills inspired their minutiae of design. Amflow just lets the power and performance do the talking.

A capable-looking bike that hides its e-bike battery and motor well. Handsome, not beautiful.

It’s solid without being harsh, stiff enough to work at the bike park but still supple enough to ride in the slop. Amflow has been sensible where it needs to - the suspension design and component choices - but hugely creative where it can with the motor.

Astonishing performance. Nothing else out there can touch this bike on the climbs, and it’s both thrilling and flattering on the descents.

A bike with this much power and battery capacity should not weigh this little - at 21.4kg it’s in the sweet spot to generate grip without feeling heavy,

This bike costs a lot of money, particularly when there are alternative Amflow models for less than half this. But it’s subjective, and I think it’s good value for the performance gains.

items.title: UCI opens voting for its Fans’ Choice Awards with some surprising nominations - Who would get your vote?
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The UCI have opened voting for its Fans’ Choice Awards, which allows fans to select their riders of the year across five categories in road cycling.

Awards will be presented to the five winners at the UCI’s annual gala, which will be held in Benidorm on Wednesday, December 9. The shortlists in each category can be found below, with each consisting of 10 names, five men and five women.

The nominees include Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who has three nominations in the Feat of the Year classification, Paul Seixas (Decathlon-CMA CGM) for his win at Il Lombardia, and Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) for winning Milan-San Remo, though his fifth Tour de France win seems to have been missed.

Among the women, Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) has three nominations across the Young Rider, Domestique and Climber selections, while Vuelta Femenina winner Paula Blasi (UAE Team L'IMAD) was nominated in the Young and Climbers lists. Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) is nominated only for winning stage 1 of the Tour de France, though her other 23 wins aren't mentioned.

World number one ranked rider Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) was nominated for her victory in Liège-Bastogne-Liège but not the Tour de France or her incredible win in Montreal at the World Championships.

And, while Mathys Rondel's nomination in the Young Rider Performance of the Year category for his GC placings at Paris-Nice and the Tour of the Alps is correct, he is also mentioned as finishing 10th in the Giro d'Italia, when in fact he was 11th.

The UCI Gala is an annual event which celebrates the season and awards the best riders, teams and nations based on the World Rankings, with the fans’ awards a new addition, giving you a voice.

"Riders write the story of every season, but it is among the fans, at the roadside and in front of their screens, that it truly resonates," UCI President David Lappartient said. "It was only natural to give them a voice. The rankings tell us who was strongest; the UCI Fans’ Choice Awards will tell us which moments meant the most to the public."

The awards ceremony will be held at the Centro Cultural de Benidorm and will be broadcast live on the UCI’s YouTube Channel.

Voting opened at 12:00 CET on Wednesday and closes on Tuesday, December 1 at 11:59 pm.

Awarded to the most remarkable individual performance in a single race

  • Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) - Classica San Sebastián; Tour de France stage 15; World Championships Time Trial

items.title: Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro review: A modern aero package but it badly needs a change of seatpost
items.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
items.content:
7.3kg(cages, no pedals or computer mount)

SRAM Red, Shimano Dura-Ace, Ultegra

Scope x Atten Artech 6.A+

We first saw the new Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro back in August 2025 for a wind tunnel test when we had a paintless, lacquerless, menacing looking thing that seemed fresh off the factory floor. It was somewhat overshadowed that day by us also having a prototype version of the Factor ONE in the tunnel (yes, we were very smug), but nevertheless it caused enough of a stir at the time and hence to have at least piqued my interest.

Fastforward a year, and in order to review it properly, I took it on an extended trip home to Cornwall to see my family, where I sniffed out some familiar roads to calm my soul on the clifftops, and a few fresh sections to hunt out rare flat roads, where it does tend to shine. It is a fabulous place to ride, but absolutely murderous if you want an easy day out.

Reviewing it as I did straight after hopping off the fabulous Look 795 Blade RS - to be published in the coming days - left it with a tough act to follow, and one it didn’t quite manage to live up to. It certainly isn’t without merit though, and while I don’t necessarily think it’s quite up there with the absolute cream of the best road bikes (or indeed the best aero road bikes), it is certainly a good bicycle, and may well suit your tastes more than it does mine. Ultimately the front end felt a little languid for my tastes, but more presingly the combination of a slack-ish seat tube angle and a 20mm setback seat post stuck me in what felt like a rather old school position out of step with the modern era.

As always, let's tackle the subjective subject of how the thing looks first; I’m a fan. It manages to toe the line of looking hyper-modern without going absolutely bananas like the Factor ONE, with clear cues from TT bike design. Those hefty, extremely dropped seat stays would be just at home on the brand’s triathlon machines. Ridley also helped everyone out by normalising massive headtubes with the Noah Fast 3.0, something the Nitrogen Pro has up front to go with a relatively wide-set fork that’ll handle 34mm as measured tyres, which is a capacity matched at the back end.

While it can handle a 34 it comes with 30c Vittoria Corsa Pros on Scope Artech 6.A wheels, but not the standard set that I had the pleasure of riding on the Look Blade; these are a collaboration with Scope and Atten, Argon’s in-house componentry brand, and the extremely fast wheels have been reshaped to better suit the 30mm tyres and to better interact with the frameset, all while keeping the Scope hubs and that eye-catching fish scale texture. In reality they feel no different to the standard Artechs, but it is heartening to know they’ve at least been optimised to this machine in particular.

Back up front and you get the same CHB-01 cockpit as is found on the brand’s Anti Matter aero gravel bike that my colleague Tom loved so much. This you can spec when you buy it in either a 36cm or a 38cm width, and with a choice of stem lengths from 80-130mm at no extra charge.

What you cannot do is spec a zero offset seatpost, which is something I believe you should not only to do but also something you do. I’ll go into the why in a sec, but if you do want to do this it’ll cost you a cool £225.

Geometrically I do want to start at the back end. The seat post is pretty set back; 1 full degree slacker than the Look Blade. This is compounded by having a full 20mm setback seatpost, rather than a 13mm on the Look. It is the same as on a Tarmac however, though again with a less severe seatpost setback from Specialized.

Without boring you too much with maths, for my saddle height a 1 degree change in seat tube angle (STA) equates to roughly 13mm of increased saddle setback. Add in the 7mm differential in the seat posts and the Argon puts me a full 20mm further behind the BB; potentially manageable if you run your saddle in the middle of the rails but as someone who has theirs slammed forwards I would have needed a costly swap.

This is all compared to somewhat ‘normal’ geometry bikes. The seat tube angle is 1.5 degrees slacker than a progressive Ridley Noah, and a full three degrees slacker than the Factor ONE, though these are a lot more radical and not everyday machines.

Before I jump two-footed into the aerodynamics, it’s worth remembering the Nitrogen comes in two guises; the Pro, which I have with a lighter, stiffer carbon layup and more pricey build options, and the standard model with lower tier components and carbon, but ultimately the same aerodynamic shape.

With a rider on, at the time of testing it proved to be reasonably fast. Since then, though, we have been fortunate enough to test a load of other new releases, and it isn’t quite as fast as many of them, now sitting around ⅔ of the way down our power rankings of road bikes. While you should obviously read all of our wind tunnel content, and the one pertaining to the test in which the Nitrogen Pro was included, it’s worth bearing in mind that while ‘bottom third’ sounds bad, it is only shipping 7.5 watts to a Cervélo S5 in reality. If you need every watt then this may be of concern to you, but it’s perfectly plausible you could make this up elsewhere, though you could also make up that deficit elsewhere have a faster bike.

It’s easy to perhaps look at ‘bottom third in the wind tunnel rankings’ and conclude that this is a slow bike, but it isn’t really. Seven and a half watts is measurable, though only barely perceptible, and on the flats the Nitrogen Pro feels very much at home once you settle into a decent position, though as with so much of the performance of the machine the thing that seems to be holding it back is mostly down to the position it puts you in.

Having a relatively slack seat tube angle combined with a 20mm setback post means you do feel like you’re hanging off the back of the bike. On the flats, while the bike is certainly aero enough, it lacks that feeling of efficiency that comes with being more over the front of the bike. My hips felt impinged, and more than anything else it just felt quite old school.

On the flat it lacked that feeling of biomechanical efficiency (though it felt aerodynamically so), and on the climbs where your weight is naturally going to be further back I felt I had to spend more time on the tops than in the hoods just because that’s where my weight fell. When out of the saddle, either on climbs or in a sprint, these problems dissipated immediately, but that isn’t a sustainable solution. A shorter stem may have helped a touch, but only in terms of the overall reach and not what’s going on at the hips. Basically it needs a zero offset seatpost, and I think you should factor it into the cost of the machine.

I don’t think I’m alone; I did a basic straw poll (Instagram stalk) of Argon sponsored athletes. Chris Hall, Rasmus Bøgh Wallin, Linus Østdal, and the riders from Team Cranks appear to be on zero setback posts. It isn’t exclusive, and some other athletes weren’t, but from what I can see from a brief search it seems the majority are opting for the option to get them over the front of the bike.

Up front I found the fact my weight was off the back more than I’d like, combined with a slacker head tube angle (0.8º slacker than Tarmac, for example) meant the front end felt a little more languid and slow than I’d like, particularly at slow speeds. Moreover, being over the back means less weight over the front wheel, meaning reduced front end grip. This is, again, solvable with a costly seatpost swap, though only to a point; the head angle ain’t going to change. That being said, if you want a road bike that errs towards stability rather than waspish agility then this could well be a machine for you. On the twisty lanes of Cornwall I often found myself wishing I was on something a little more reactive, but on the flip side if you relish longer, steadier efforts on flat or rolling terrain (once you lock the position in) I think this would be a very decent machine.

At 7.5kg in this spec it’s not a superlight hillclimb machine but there’s a lot of carbon in the frame, forks and in those deep Scope wheels. It doesn’t have the immediacy of acceleration on steeper gradients that you get with bikes around the UCI weight limit (or below), but it’s also not absolutely leaden either. Certainly one more for fast, rolling terrain but if anyone tells me they can’t bear to ride a 7.5kg machine in the mountains I will tell them to go and touch some grass.

Sprints… now we’re talking. That super-compact rear triangle with large, boxy stays in combination with a bottom bracket shell that’s tall enough to sit proud of the outer front chainring just gobble up high wattage efforts and there’s no concerning play in the cockpit at all. I’d have like the tops to sweep forward a little sooner; the right angle transition is quite sharp and can sometimes leave your forearms contacting the bars when you're sprinting in the drops, particularly uphill, but it’s a minor quibble, and not something I cared too much about while bagging a few local, extremely low hanging ego-massaging KOMs.

The Nitrogen Pro, in this spec at least, is a funny old beast from a value perspective and is a little like the Force-equipped Factor Elara I reviewed recently. Everything besides the groupset is top drawer and as you would get on the best-of-the-best model, so you can look at it two ways: either you’re getting basically the performance of a £12,500 bike for £9,500 ($10,499), where a saving of three thousand pounds to Dura-Ace is significant, or you can look at it as £9.5k being a lot for an Ultegra-spec bike. An Ultegra Specialized Tarmac (not the S-Works, which this ‘Pro’ Nitrogen is more akin to) is £3.5k cheaper, but has less fizzy wheels, a separate cockpit, and it doesn’t say S-Works on the downtube.

Personally I actually like this new trend of top tier bikes but with a downrated groupset. Aside from weight, Ultegra is basically indistinguishable from Dura-Ace and Force is essentially the same as Red so it saves a huge wad of cash for a negligible performance hit.

Setback seatpost aside, as this is a problem that I think can be alleviated at a small cost, I think it accounts for itself reasonably well. Extremely fast wheels tuned to the frame and tyres, which themselves are a modern 30c width and not a cheaper option to bring the price down. A decent cockpit, and a stiff package that is pretty aerodynamic in the grand scheme of things, even if it isn’t world beating.

As tested I think there’s a lot to be positive about with the Argon 18 Nitrogen Pro. It’s stiff, an excellent sprinter, and while the handling isn’t lively enough for my liking it is certainly acceptable if you prefer something a little more stable and forgiving rather than hair raising and spicy. I think it’s a bike that, with a change of seatpost that I think is more of a necessity than an option despite the added cost, would be a fine mile munching fast bike for rolling and flat terrain.

I think if you’re looking for something of a do-it-all fast bike then you will perhaps have a better time with something with more of an all-rounder feel.

Looks good. Under the space age looks there isn't a great deal groundbreaking going on however, but neither is there anything crazy and superfluous.

Just a groupset away from top spec. Own brand Scopes are fun, that's for sure.

Perfectly acceptable for a chunky aero bike with big wheels.

The aero is decent in the grand scheme of things, though not world beating, but the geometry has too many implications for me to have truly fallen in love with the thing.

Top tier but with a step down in groupset can be viewed a couple of ways. I think it's a good entry point into superbike performance, but it's not an absolute bargain. Also you have to buy a new seatpost if you want an inline.
